content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors point out three requirements on industrial-driven attack detector: R1: black-box scenario, R2: low resources/computation time, R3: no oracle on the nature of the attackers. With that, they design the first efficient adversarial attacks detector that meets all the requirements. With comprehensive evaluation, their new design can outperform the existing works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Propose a novel designs that can satisfy the three requirements
- Perform comprehensive  evaluation of their methodology on different datasets and attacks

Weakness:
- The motivation is not well-supported due to a lack of justification for their three requirements.
In the paper, the authors are motivated by real-world systems such as face recognition systems and autonomous driving systems. With that, they propose three requirements of the real-life scenarios for adversarial detections and claim that all the existing methods fail to meet these requirements. However, in this paper, they do not provide justification for these three requirements. Without support or justification on real-world systems, it is very difficult to judge whether these requirements are biased or not. Previous work cannot meet these requirements maybe because it is a real requirement and the majority of existing work is already good enough to work in real-world systems. Since this paper is motivated by the real-world system, I would recommend the authors to perform some survey study on what industry needs for such systems. Without the justification or support of their motivation, it is very difficult to judge the significance of this work.

- Lack of practicality evaluation.
This paper is motivated by the real-world systems I mentioned above but later on there is no evaluation of the practicality. The main evaluations are purely on three benchmarks (CIFAR 10, CIFAR 100, and Tiny ImageNet). The authors should consider evaluating on more realistic/high-resolution datasets such as ImageNet. Otherwise, they could also justify that these three datasets are used for real-world systems. Due to the practical motivation, it would be great if the authors could evaluate their design in a real-world system or at least in more realistic/practical settings. Otherwise, it is very difficult to judge whether their design can be applied to real-world systems. Also, it would be better if the authors could discuss more on what actions the system should behave after the detections. For a real-time system such as the autonomous vehicle mentioned in the paper, usually, detection of the attack alone is not enough due to its high safety critical property. Thus, if this paper is motivated by such systems, they should provide more designs or descriptions.

- Lack of discussion or comparison with the related work.
Certified robustness is currently one of the most powerful defenses for adversarial attacks recently, which provides the provable guarantee of the models. For instance, "SoK: Certified Robustness for Deep Neural Networks" published in IEEE S&P 2023 provides a systematic study of the existing certified robustness methods. If we can already prove that the DNN is robust, their new design may not be that useful. With that, the R3 shown in the paper is not held for the real-world system. The authors should discuss such related works in their paper and argue why it is necessary to still have their new designs.

Minor issue:
- Typo in the introduction "scenarii"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is easy to read and follow. The designs also look novel. But I just have major concerns on the motivation, evaluation, and literature review.

- It does not have a well-supported/solid motivation
- Motivated by practical real-world systems but no evaluations
- Lack of discussion/comparison on related works

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper tackles the problem of detection of adversarial attacks in “real-world” settings. The paper begins by arguing that real-world deployments of deep learning (DL) for computer vision (CV) must satisfy 3 “self-proposed” requirements (R). Then, the authors show that, among existing detection methods, only 7 meet R3 (i.e., they can detect adversarial examples not seen during their training phase); of these, only 2 meet R1 (i.e., they assume that the attacker has only black-box access to the targeted DL system). The remaining 2 are then assessed on R2, which demands that a detector must have a low inference time. The paper then proposes “REFEREE”, a detection method that arguably addresses all 3 requirements. The proposed method is empirically validated on CIFAR10/100 and TinyImageNet, and is shown to be faster than past methods. The evaluation also includes additional analyses, such as interpretability, detection rate, as well as ablation studies and experiments against “adaptive” attackers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
STRENGTHS:
+ Section 2 is interesting: showing which papers meet (or not) a given requirement can be useful for practitioners
+ The intuition is interesting 
+ Interpretability and Ablation studies are interesting
+ Some analyses are intriguing

WEAKNESSES
- Unfair Self-claims (i.e., lack of supporting evidence for the requirements)
- The requirements are poorly formulated
- The literature review is not exhaustive
- Subpar writing
- Poor theoretical foundation
- Unclear amount of trials performed
- Results are not practical
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the presentation of the paper is mediocre (I believe the first three sections are the worst part of the paper).

The quality of the English text is mediocre.

Figures and Tables are appropriate.

The topic addressed by the manuscript is trendy and well-known, but relevant for ICLR.

The references are not appropriate.

The contribution is not very significant.

The underlying idea of the paper draws from a well-known method, but which has not been yet employed in this domain. Specifically, the intuition borrows the “information projection” as a means to derive the “anomaly score” used to detect an adversarial example. Such a methodology is – to the best of my knowledge – not common in related literature. Hence, from the novelty perspective, the proposed method is “novel”.

The results are reproducible: the data is public and the code is provided in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I do not recommend this paper for acceptance, as it is affected by multiple and crucial issues that (I believe) do not make the paper as a strong contender for ICLR. However – I want to emphasize this – the paper is not devoid of merit. For this, I commend the authors: the underlying intuition and the huge variety of experiments were interesting to read, and I truly endorse the authors in continuing their line of research on this subject. Therefore, in what follows, I will thoroughly explain all the major reasons that led me to believe that the paper is (currently) inadequate for ICLR; but I will also provide actionable suggestions that I would love the authors to make. I truly look forward to reading a more polished (and "scientific") version of this paper.

(I will engage in the discussion, but I must warn the authors that it is unlikely that I will change my decision on this paper, as the amount of effort to make it into an acceptable state for ICLR goes beyond what can be done in the short timeframe of the rebuttal phase)

**Unfair Self claims.**
Let me quote a sentence from the introduction: “In this paper, we introduce the first efficient adversarial attacks detector that meets all requirements (R1) - (R2) - (R3) of real-life applications of computer vision.” This sentence appears very enticing, but it is also unfair. First, “all requirements” is misleading: such requirements are “self-declared” in this very paper, and are provided with only 3 lines (at most) of descriptive content. In other words, the paper states “there are 3 requirements, and our method meets all of them”, which is rather convenient (and unscientific). Especially because the paper attempts to do so for “any” real life application of computer vision. Such a phrasing is unacceptable for ICLR, and this fact alone makes me lean towards rejection. Do note that a justification for any of R1-2-3 is not provided anywhere in the paper. While I acknowledge that some of such requirements are sensible, they are far from being “universal” requirements – and even if they were, a better and rigorous motivation and explanation should be provided. I invite the authors to look at [C, D] for recent works that attempt a similar objective as the one in this submission.

**Poorly formulated requirements.**
The requirements are poorly formulated. This has to do with the “poor writing quality” that I already mentioned. Put simply, in their current formulation, the requirements are not detailed enough to be considered as “scientific”. For instance, R2 demands a low computation time, but it does not provide any clear definition of what “low” actually means. As a consequence, it is unfair to claim that “our method meets R2, while Xu et al. (2018) and Meng & Chen (2017) do not” on the sole basis that “our method is faster”. At the same time, for R1 it is not clear what is referred to as “end-user”. My understanding is that R1 refers to the traditional “black-box setting”, wherein an “attacker” must evade a system without having any form of knowledge of its internal workflow. However, it could also be that the “black-box setting” is from the “defender” perspective, i.e., the developers of the detection system do not know anything about the DL system to protect. I this case, however, I call that this requirement is flawed: it is entirely within the realm of possibility that the developers of a DL model will also be interested in protecting such model with a detector of adversarial attacks --- and, of course, such developers are well-aware of the internal configuration of the DL model. For this reason, I will interpret R1 as describing the former case.

**Poor literature review.**
Although I liked Section 2.2, there is little in this Section that makes me believe that the authors included all “relevant” methods, as only 10 previous papers are referenced (and, of these, only 2 are published after 2020). The impression is that the paper cherry picked those prior works that better gave credit to the paper’s thesis, i.e., that no work meets all the (self-declared) requirements. Again, I point the authors to [C, D] for some guides on how fairly perform a literature review that can show that the problem “exists”, and that is not based just on self-claims.

**Poor theoretical foundations.**
Ultimately, REFEREE is an anomaly detector: it takes a sample, computes an anomaly score, and then uses a threshold to determine whether the sample is “malicious or benign”. The main intuition/novelty is to leverage the concept of “Information Projection”, introduced by Kullback (1997); Csisz´ar (1975; 1984). While such concept is well-known (albeit not in the specific context of detection of adversarial examples), the paper does not provide a sound theoretical analysis that demonstrates that such a method “works in general”. In other words, while I do acknowledge that the underlying intuition is sensible, validating whether REFEREE is good or not is simply left to an empirical assessment. I invite the authors to provide a strong theoretical argument in favor of REFEREE: sure, it works on two datasets (in the testbed created by the authors), but will it equally work “in any real-world deployment of DL for CV”, as claimed by the paper? Such a question cannot be answered with the provided information.

**Flawed evaluation (or Requirement).**
According to (my interpretation of) R1, the detection system assumes an attacker who has black-box access to the targeted DL model. However, in the evaluation, the papers considers a wide-array of attacks that are white-box. This is a clear violation of (my interpretation of) R1; meaning that either all such results are useless, or that R1 is flawed in the first place (see my comment about “vague requirements”).

**Unclear amount of trials performed**
The “improvements” of REFEREE over previous methods do not appear to be “statistically validated”. Indeed, doing so requires to perform multiple (and fair) trials, and then performing a proper comparison. For instance, let me quote the caption of Table 4: “Mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) are obtained by aggregating results by Lp-norm”. I appreciate including such information, but it is not clear what is actually being aggregated. Furthermore, the impression is that the evaluation is carried out by evaluating everything only once – this also includes the computational time. 

**Results are not practical**
One of the biggest issues for “real” practitioners is false positives. Unfortunately, the proposed method – according to the results shown in the paper – triggers a vast amount of false positives. From a practical perspective, a detector with over 20% FPR is unusable. Personally, I believe that practitioners are more interested in “low false positives” than “low inference time” (w.r.t. R2).

**Subpar writing**
The paper is readable, but the overall writing quality is lackluster. Specifically, some sentences are redundant or confusing, and typos frequently occur. I endorse the authors to revise the entire text of the paper with the assistance of a native speaker. Below I will list some issues that affect the Abstract and the Introduction (boldface denotes the most problematic ones):

•	I did not really understand the meaning of R1 and R3 stated in the abstract. Actually, while I found R1 to be just confusing, I believe that R3 is plain wrong “in general”: why would a detector not require any training phase? Of course, that is “obviously true” if such a detector does not have a training phase (i.e., because it is entirely based on handcrafted rules), but this is far from being acceptable given that the sentence starts with “any detector”.

•	Abstract: “out extensive experiments demonstrates” typo

•	Abstract: “REFEREE improves upon existing methods while considerably reducing the inference time: it requires less than 0.05 seconds by test input, which is up to 400 times faster than former methods” Just state that “experiments show that REFEREE has a 400x faster inference time than former methods”. 

•	Abstract: “This makes REFEREE an excellent candidate for adversarial attacks detection in real-world applications.” Remove this subjective statement

•	Introduction: “fueled their wide adoption in the industry.” Please provide some references. 

•	Introduction: “This paper focuses on a specific safety issue: adversarial attacks.” The term “safety” is incorrect

•	Introduction: “The latter refer to the design of malicious attackers able to craft samples that fool a given classifier.” This sentence does not make any sense.

•	Introduction: “This is typically done by adding small additive perturbations to real-world examples,” what does “adding an additive perturbation” mean? Moreover, what does the “real-world” term mean here? Does it mean that the perturbation must be added “in the real world” (e.g., putting a “post-it” to a stop sign)? Or that the sample must be taken from the “real world” (in which case, I would ask “what makes a sample not from the real world”?)?

•	Introductoin: “which are indistinguishable to human eyes but highly disruptive to network predictions.” The perturbation being “indistinguishable to human eyes” is **not a strict requirement for adversarial attacks.** See [A, B]

•	Introduction: “However, this approach contains two important limitations: (i) in many situation, it makes the training phase unstable and (ii) it is not able to anticipate for future attack mechanisms which could fool the system.” **These are very strong claims that are completely unsupported.** The authors should either add a proper explanation (or anticipate that an explanation will be given in the paper), or provide strong references to works that support such claims.

•	Introduction “design of detectors that are able to decide, based on an already existing system, whether an input sample is a malicious attack or not” What does “based on an already existing system” mean? I think this sentence is redundant and confusing, and invite the authors to remove it.

•	Introduction: “existing methods fail to meet the requirements of real-life scenarii” The plural of “scenario” is “scenarios”. Even by concocting a new latin term, i.e., “scenarium”, the plural would be “scenaria”. 

•	Introduction: “Systems already deployed in production are generally opaque to the end user” who is this “end user”? Note that this “issue” stems from the **lack of a clear use-case** already implicitly mentioned earlier (i.e., when I asked to provide some references of “wide adoption in industry”).

•	Introduction: “In many real-world applications, AI systems are making real-time predictions at a high frequency (e.g. face recognition for airport security). As a result, any relevant detector should have a low inference time and require low computation resources.” The simple fact that this sentence begins with “in many” invalidates using such a statement to support a “requirement” that should be applicable to “any” real-world scenario. “Many” is not “all”; this is a lack of rigour.

•	Introduction: “Any relevant detector should be unsupervized, meaning it should not require any training phase with access to attack examples” First, “unsupervized” should be “unsupervised”. Second, I still do not agree with this remark (as also stated in my comment on RQ3 in the Abstract). Perhaps a better wording should be that “a detector should work against unknown attacks, whose samples are not seen during its training phase”. But this is a significantly different concept than stating that the detector does not require any training phase.

Minor:
•	On page 5, the text reports “our REFEREE can be divided into three steps”, but in the box I only see two steps.

•	The paper proposes a “detector” of (adversarial) attacks. However, there is no description of the envisioned threat model. I invite the authors to look into [E].


EXTERNAL REFERENCES

[A]: Schneider "Concept-based Adversarial Attacks: Tricking Humans and Classifiers Alike." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy Workshops (2022).

[B]: Elsayed "Adversarial examples that fool both computer vision and time-limited humans." Advances in neural information processing systems 31 (2018).

[C]: Apruzzese "SoK: The Impact of Unlabelled Data in Cyberthreat Detection." IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (2022).

[D]: Arp "Dos and don’ts of machine learning in computer security." Proc. of the USENIX Security Symposium. 2022.

[E]: Biggio "Wild patterns: Ten years after the rise of adversarial machine learning." Pattern Recognition 84 (2018)

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose REFREE, an adversarial example detector based on the Tsallis divergence, leveraging the intuition that adversarial examples are out-of-distribution samples. The authors add the notion of the training data distribution to compute an anomaly score that triggers the presence of a suspicious point, by taking the minimum Tsallis divergence between the output of the input sample and the training data. The authors show that REFREE outperforms other detectors in terms of standard and adaptive attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths.**
+ adversarial examples detection is an interesting problem, and tackling it from the out-of-distribution point of view is a good intuition
+ the authors correctly perform a possible adaptive attack that also address the presence of REFREE
+ the paper reads well, and it is well formatted to help the reader to better understand the content

**Weaknesses.**
+ **Realistic settings are claimed but not used.** The paper focuses a lot of attention and importance on being realistic, by defining three requirements that detectors must have. However, none of the three are then discussed when REFREE is proposed. Hence, the authors should include the discussion and why REFREE accomplishes all the requirements. The contribution is undermined, since the first part of the paper stresses about these requirements, that are then discarded entirely from page 3 (roughly) on.
+ **Selected defences for comparison are outdated.** The authors selected FS and MagNet that have been proven to be non robust, and they are old. The authors should use as a comparison novel work such as [a].
+ **Incremental contribution.** The techniques leverages the Tsallis divergence, and the contribution is given by computing it on training data. While this technical detail is a good intuition, its application is just incremental w.r.t. the state of the art.

[a] Stutz, David, Matthias Hein, and Bernt Schiele. "Confidence-calibrated adversarial training: Generalizing to unseen attacks." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020.

content.title: Adversarial Attack Detection Under Realistic Constraints
content.TL;DR: We propose a simple, real-time, softmax-based detection method for adversarial samples.
content.abstract: While adversarial attacks are a serious threat for neural networks safety, existing defense mechanisms remain very limited regarding their applicability to real-world settings. Any industrial-driven attack detector is expected to meet three unavoidable requirements: (R1) being adapted to black-box scenario where the user has only access to the predicted probabilities, (R2) making fast inference and (R3) not involving any training phase. In this paper, we introduce REFEREE, the first detector that meets all these requirements while improving state-of-the-art performances. It leverages the concept of information projections (I-projection), which generalizes ideas coming from out-of-distribution detection and allows to extract relevant information contained in the softmax outputs of a network. Our extensive experiments demonstrates that REFEREE improves upon existing methods while considerably reducing the inference time: it requires less than 0.05 seconds by test input, which is up to 400 times faster than former methods. This makes REFEREE an excellent candidate for adversarial attacks detection in real-world applications.
